concept.name: Policy rate
concept.definition: The short-term interest rate that a central bank sets (or targets) to implement monetary policy. In the United States it is the Federal Open Market Committee's target range for the federal funds rate, which the New York Fed's trading desk defends through open market operations and administered rates.
concept.intuition: It is the central bank's main dial: raising it tightens financial conditions to cool the economy, lowering it loosens conditions to stimulate activity.
concept.mechanics: The FOMC announces a target range for the federal funds rate; the Desk conducts repo, reverse repo, and other operations, and sets administered rates (interest on reserve balances, ON RRP offering rate, standing repo rate) to keep the effective market rate within the range.
concept.failure_modes: The policy rate directly anchors only very short-term rates; long-term yields are driven by expectations and term premia, so policy moves can fail to transmit (e.g. the 2000s 'conundrum' when long yields fell as the Fed hiked). At the zero lower bound, the rate loses room as a tool.
concept.misconceptions: The central bank does not 'set all interest rates'; it targets one overnight rate and influences the rest of the curve only indirectly through expectations and operations.
concept.example: In 2022–2023 the FOMC raised its target range for the federal funds rate from 0–0.25% to 5.25–5.50% in a series of moves of 25 to 75 basis points.
